title: The little scroll (Revelation 10)
hook: sweet as honey in the mouth, bitter in the stomach

segments.voice: Yesterday, the seventh seal opened and heaven went quiet for half an hour. Your line was silence in heaven. Where did you find a quiet stretch? Day one thousand three hundred two.

An angel comes down wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head. He plants his right foot on the sea and his left foot on the land, and he cries out like a lion roaring. Seven thunders answer him. John reaches for his pen to write down what they said, and a voice stops him: seal it up, and don't write it. So there are words in Revelation that Revelation keeps to itself. Then the voice gives a stranger order. Go to the angel and take the little book open in his hand. John walks up and asks for it. The angel hands it over and says: eat it. That little book is today's word.
screen: `ONE FOOT ON THE SEA, ONE ON THE LAND.`

segments.voice: The King James calls it a little book. The title here says little scroll. Either way, it's something with words in it, small enough to hold in one hand. First, the warning comes before the meal. The angel says, in the King James words: "it shall make thy belly bitter, but it shall be in thy mouth sweet as honey." John eats it anyway, and it's exactly as promised: "it was in my mouth sweet as honey: and as soon as I had eaten it, my belly was bitter." Second, John isn't alone in eating his message. Ezekiel was handed a scroll, and on it were written "lamentations, and mourning, and woe." He ate it too, and he says: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." A scroll full of grief, and it tasted like honey. John's story leans on Ezekiel's. Third, why bitter? The text doesn't say outright, so readers differ. Some hear it about the calling: God's word is sweet to receive and heavy to carry, because the very next line is an order: "Thou must prophesy again before many peoples, and nations, and tongues, and kings." Others hear it about the message itself: news of God's victory, and news of the suffering still on the way, in one mouthful. Fourth, this isn't only a vision. Plenty of true things land this way. A diagnosis that finally explains the pain. An honest word from a friend. A calling you know is yours, and know will cost you. Sweet to hear, and then it has to go all the way down.

Here's the practice: notice a truth that's both sweet and hard. Settle, and breathe. Let one come to mind. Something you know is true about your life, your family, your work, that's good to know and hard to carry. Don't fix it. Just hold it, the way John held the little book before he ate it. Notice where the sweet part is. Notice where the hard part sits in your body. If you pray, you can bring both to God at once. If you don't, simply let both be true together for a minute. The bell holds the time.
The little scroll. The book John was told to eat in Revelation ten: sweet as honey in his mouth, bitter once it was inside him.

Your line: sweet and bitter. This week took us from a knock at the door in Laodicea, through a throne, a Lamb, four riders and a crowd from every nation, into silence, and now a book you eat. Today, when a true word is hard to swallow, notice the honey in it too. Day one thousand three hundred two.

howItsDone: Christians who read Revelation 10 alongside Ezekiel 2–3 often hear it as a picture of receiving God's word: preachers and readers speak of taking scripture in slowly, letting it become part of them, sweet and demanding at once.
